newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore ruling party rolls over key foe.
newsitem.headline: Singapore ruling party rolls over key foe.

text.p: Singapore's opposition parties retained at least two seats but the ruling party's juggernaut rolled over one of its main opponents as results came in from Thursday's general election.
Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and his People's Action Party were assured in advance of retaining power because opponents contested only 36 of parliament's 83 seats.
It was not yet clear early Friday whether the opposition would match or improve on the four seats they won in the last election.
Chee Soon Juan, leader of the Singapore Democratic Party, failed to capture a key seat, winning only a third of the vote after a campaign in which government leaders branded him a "proven liar".

But Chiam See Tong, the former SDP chief who lost a leadership battle with Chee, helped prevent a PAP clean sweep, scraping home with a reduced majority under the banner of his new Singapore People's Party.
The Worker's Party kept the one seat it had in the old parliament.

With results mostly as expected after the brief nine-day election campaign, attentioned was focused on a winner-take-all race in the five-member constituency of Cheng San, which analysts rated as the Worker's Party's best hope of making gains.
The result there would decide whether the PAP's grip on parliament was slightly weakened or made tighter still.
Prime Minister Goh made clear from the outset of the campaign that he would consider any opposition win a setback.

The opposition had wanted the campaign to focus on issues like a rising cost of living and that parliament should have some non-PAP voice, but had little chance to get its message across as PAP successfully controlled the election agenda.
Of the four opposition seats won at last election, three were taken by the SDP. All have now changed hands -- Chiam's to his new party and the others captured by the PAP on Thursday.

Chee, not a member of parliament, was found in contempt of the assembly last year after complaining to one of its committees that the government share of health care spending was down to five percent.
He later admitted it should have been 25 percent, and put the mistake down to a typing error. But he was subjected to a major PAP campaign against his character.
Goh also turned the PAP big guns on in Cheng San, picking out "Chinese chauvinist" Tang Liang Hong of the Worker's Party as the principal target of the whole election campaign.
He accused Tang of seeking Chinese domination of multi-racial Singapore, evoking still-strong memories of racial riots in the 1960s.
Goh put his prestige on the line in Cheng San, telling the electorate that if they voted for Tang they risked throwing away three decades of racial harmony.
Singapore is 77 percent ethnic Chinese with significant minorities of Malays and Tamils but uses English as its working language to avoid the possibility of one dominating.
To reinforce the message, state television's election coverage was in English, Mandarin, Malay and Tamil, with reporters speaking consecutively.

In his determination to defeat the WP in Cheng San, Goh also used the formidable weapon of multi-billion dollar housing estate renovations, telling voters there bluntly that if they voted against the PAP they would go to the back of the line.
That campaign tactic, in which Goh said opposition precincts would end up as slums in elegant, modern Singapore, brought criticism from the United States.
Goh protested angrily that Washington was interfering in what was a perfectly normal election campaign.
